$comment: Shared fact conformance vectors (PR 4, #156). Every category is an array of { input, expected }, except languageSpecific, which is keyed by language (each language block holds arrays of the same shape, run with that language's string literal decoder). canonicalNumber: expected null means not a constant (canonicalNumber returns undefined). Not constants: names, strings, division by zero, a decimal integer literal with a leading zero other than 0 itself (017), a division of two integer operands with a non-zero remainder (7 / 2; an operand is integer when it is an integer literal or an expression of integer operands; 7.0 / 2 is a float division), results with |v| >= 2^53, and a non-zero result that rounds to 0 at 6 decimals. An integer result prints as plain digits; any other result is the exact binary double rounded to 6 decimals, as JS toFixed(6) does: 0.0000005 is the double 4.99999999999999977e-7, so it rounds to 0 and is not a constant, and 0.0000015 gives 0.000002; an exact tie (0.0078125) rounds half away from zero (0.007813, -0.007813). Trailing zeros are removed and -0 prints 0. Java copies must round with new BigDecimal(double).setScale(6, RoundingMode.HALF_UP), never String.format("%.6f") or BigDecimal.valueOf; Go copies must not rely on strconv.FormatFloat for exact ties, which it rounds to even (0.007812). isTrivialLiteral: a number literal is evaluated as in canonicalNumber and the double is compared exactly with the list's numbers (0.9999999 is not 1). The shared rules decode only a plain double-quoted string literal (and a plain single-quoted char literal) with the common escapes (a backslash before a double quote, a single quote, a backslash, n, t or r); any other escape makes it not a constant. Every other string form (prefixes, suffixes, verbatim, interpolated, raw, single-quoted or template strings) goes to the language's string literal decoder; without one it is not a string constant, so it is never trivial (see isTrivialLiteralCustom). languageSpecific.<language> vectors run with that language's decoder (C#: decodeCsharpStringLiteral). hasRetryTimeoutFragment: tokens are ASCII only (A-Z, a-z, 0-9); every other character separates tokens; no Unicode case tests and no locale-dependent lowercasing. matchesNormalizationPattern: an absent qualifier means the call has no receiver (written Name(...)). Categories without a list in their input use the defaults block. normalizeFactText and capFactValue: input and expected are segment arrays, concatenated; a segment is a string or { repeat, count }. detailLiteral: the finisher's detail.literal for a comparison literal (same segment arrays); CRLF and CR become LF before capFactValue, so the committed index does not depend on a checkout's line endings. FC-4b (normalization that is not a business rule): isMessageSink and isDisplayCall take { callee, consumerTypes? }: the callee of the nearest call that receives the value as source text (a construction is "new <Type>"), and the types a full tier resolved for it (qualified, type arguments dropped; Go: the package path or <path>.<type>); without types the rules go by names. isTechnicalNormalization takes { method, qualifier, text } of a normalization call; feedsNormalization takes { inner, outer, outerMethod }: the inner normalization is the receiver or, except for comparison methods, the only argument of the outer one (whitespace ignored).

go.$comment: Run with decodeGoStringLiteral: a raw string `...` is its text as written, with no escapes and every carriage return removed (Go spec); interpreted "..." strings and rune literals go through the shared rules, so an escape they do not know (\x41, \u0041) is not a constant.

typescript.$comment: Run with decodeTypescriptStringLiteral: single-quoted strings and templates without substitutions, with the common escapes plus \` and \$ in templates (a CRLF line break in a template is \n); a template with a substitution, a tagged template and any other escape (\u0041, \x41) are not constants.

java.$comment: Run with decodeJavaStringLiteral: text blocks (JLS 3.10.6). The opening """ must be followed by optional spaces, tabs or form feeds and a line break; the content up to the first unescaped """ (which must end the literal) gets LF line breaks, then String.stripIndent (the last line counts toward the indentation even when blank, so a closing delimiter on its own line keeps the final newline, and one at column 0 keeps all indentation; each whitespace character, a tab included, counts as one; trailing whitespace is removed), then String.translateEscapes (\b \t \n \f \r \s \" \' \\, octal \0 to \377, a backslash before a line break joins the lines). A Unicode escape (\u0041) and any other escape are not constants, as in the shared rules. Plain "..." strings never reach the decoder ("\s" is not a constant). Int overflow (24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 365) is decided by the JDT evidence step, not by these rules: an int-typed step outside the int range gives no evidence, also inside floating arithmetic (1.5 * 2 * (100000 * 100000)). Hex, octal and binary int literals above INT_MAX without L (0xFFFFFFFF, 037777777777, 0b followed by 32 ones) are valid Java ints with wrapped values (0xFFFFFFFF is -1), while the shared rules read them unsigned (4294967295), so they are not constants: the evidence step drops a binding or duration amount holding one, and a comparison or case label whose number literal is one gives no evidence (so no fact). The syntax tier (Task 7) applies the same rules from the literals alone. In a flattened chain the int steps before the first floating operand are checked (100000 * 100000 * 1.5 overflows); from a floating first operand on, Java computes in double (1.5 * 100000 * 100000 does not). overflowsInt vectors: a Java expression and whether the JDT evidence step treats it as not a constant (types from the literals: an integer literal without L is an int). comparisonGivesEvidence vectors: a comparison of an int x inside an if condition and whether it gives comparison evidence.
